concepts.def: Pre-1914 alignments: Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy) and Triple Entente (Britain, France, Russia).
Diplomatic breakdown following Franz Ferdinand's assassination on 28 June 1914 in Sarajevo.
German strategy to defeat France via Belgium in six weeks before turning east on Russia.
Static front from late 1914 stretching from the Channel to Switzerland, dominated by machine guns and artillery.
Anglo-French offensive 1 July - 18 November 1916; British suffered 57,470 casualties on day one.
1919 peace imposing on Germany territorial losses, GBP 6.6 billion reparations and Article 231 war guilt.

walkthroughs.body_html: Historians debate emphasis between Fritz Fischer's thesis of German bid for world power, structural alliance entanglements, Anglo-German naval race, Balkan instability, and contingency. Franz Ferdinand's assassination on 28 June 1914 triggered Austria's ultimatum to Serbia on 23 July. German 'blank cheque' support, Russian mobilisation on 30 July and German invasion of Belgium on 4 August produced a continental war.

The Schlieffen Plan failed at the Marne in September 1914 as French and British armies counterattacked. The 'race to the sea' established trench lines. Industrial firepower made offensives costly: Verdun (February-December 1916) inflicted 700,000 casualties; the Somme another 1.1 million. American entry in April 1917, German Spring Offensives in 1918 and the Allied Hundred Days produced armistice on 11 November 1918.

J.M. Keynes's Economic Consequences of the Peace (1919) condemned Versailles as ruinous, a view shared by Lloyd George. Revisionists like Sally Marks argue the GBP 6.6 billion reparations were affordable and German non-payment political. Margaret MacMillan emphasises the treaty's contradictions: too harsh to conciliate, too lenient to incapacitate, leaving German revisionism intact.

options: Article 231
Article 14
Article 100
Article 5

mcqs.q: Did the Treaty of Versailles directly cause WWII?
options: Versailles caused WWII because it required Germany to invade Poland.
They were a religious war between Catholics and Protestants.
Versailles caused WWII directly because it was so harsh on Germany.
It contributed via German resentment and economic strain, but the 1930s Depression, Hitler's choices, and Allied appeasement were equally necessary — Versailles alone is not sufficient.

mcqs.q: What were the Wars of the Roses really about?
options: The whole country was at war for thirty continuous years.
Dynastic conflict between rival branches of the Plantagenets (Lancaster and York) over the throne, intensified by weak kingship under Henry VI and noble factionalism.
They were a religious war between Catholics and Protestants.
The Schlieffen Plan failed because it tried to invade Russia first.

mcqs.q: Why did the Schlieffen Plan fail in 1914?
options: The Schlieffen Plan failed because it tried to invade Russia first.
Versailles caused WWII because it required Germany to invade Poland.
The Schlieffen Plan failed because Britain entered the war.
Belgian resistance delayed the German advance; Russia mobilised faster than expected; Moltke weakened the right wing; and the French rallied at the Marne.
